card.title: Table management: the arithmetic of one extra seating a night
card.excerpt: Turning a table twenty minutes faster is worth more than most marketing. Here's how to measure turnover, where the minutes hide, and what software genuinely helps with.

h1: Restaurant table management: getting a second seating out of the same room
intro: You can't add tables to a dining room, but you can serve more people at the ones you have. Most venues lose their turnover in three places — the wait before the order, the wait for the bill, and the ten minutes a table sits dirty. None of that needs new equipment. It needs knowing where the minutes go.

blocks.text: Table turnover is covers served divided by seats available in a service. If you have 40 seats and serve 60 covers on a Friday night, your turnover is 1.5.

The reason to care: at an average spend of €28, moving Friday from 1.5 to 1.8 is 12 extra covers, or €336. Do that on Friday and Saturday and it's about €2,900 a month — from the same room, the same menu and the same staff.
Time a few tables end to end and the distribution is remarkably consistent across venues:

Two columns matter. The eating time is not yours to compress — squeezing it is how you get a bad review. The two waits around it are pure dead time, and together they routinely run 20 to 30 minutes per table. That's your extra seating, sitting in plain sight.
The four fixes, in order of payback

items: **Let guests order when they're ready.** The wait for a waiter to become free is the single biggest block, and it's worst exactly when you're busiest. [Ordering from the table](route:/order-taking) removes it entirely for the venues where the style fits.
**Let guests pay when they're ready.** The bill dance costs 10 to 25 minutes. Pay-at-table collapses it to about one.
**Reset faster.** A dirty table is unsellable. Assign clearing explicitly rather than hoping; five minutes saved per table is a seating over a night.
**Stop double-seating the same server.** Two tables that sit down together both wait. Stagger seating by five minutes and both get served faster.

blocks.text: The useful version is a live floor plan: which tables are free, occupied, ordered, waiting for the bill or being reset — visible to everyone at once instead of held in the head of whoever is on the door.

items: **Status at a glance**, so a server walking past knows table 12 has been waiting since 20:40.
**Seating suggestions** — a walk-in four goes to the table that frees soonest, not the first one someone remembers.
**Table linked to the order**, so the bill, the QR order and the kitchen ticket all agree about who is sitting where.
**History**, so you can see that your Saturday second seating is consistently 25 minutes late and fix the cause.
**Reservations on the same map** as walk-ins, which is where most double-booking comes from.

blocks.text: Software doesn't turn tables. It removes the guessing that makes turning them slow. If your floor is 12 tables and one person runs it well, a whiteboard is genuinely fine — the case gets strong at around 20 tables, multiple servers, or a mix of bookings and walk-ins.

A tasting-menu restaurant selling one seating a night is not doing table management wrong; the seating is the product. A neighbourhood bar where people sit for three hours over two beers is monetising something other than the plate. Push turnover in either and you break the business you have.
A two-week measurement you can actually run

items: Pick four tables. For one week, note seating time, order time, bill request and reset-complete on a card taped under the table.
Average each gap. You'll find one that's twice what you assumed.
Change one thing only, for the following week.
Compare. Keep the change if the gap shrank and nobody complained.

blocks.text: Ask the servers where the time goes before you measure. They almost always know, and they're usually right — measurement mostly settles the argument about which of the two known problems is bigger.

blocks.heading: See your whole floor in one place
blocks.text: Live table status, orders tied to tables and reservations on the same map. 14 days free, no card required.

items.q: What is a good table turnover rate?
items.a: It depends entirely on format. Fast casual runs 3 or higher, a bistro around 1.5–2 per service, fine dining often 1. Compare yourself to your own last month, not to someone else's format.

items.q: How do I calculate table turnover?
items.a: Covers served in a service divided by the number of seats. 60 covers on 40 seats is 1.5.

items.q: Do I need software for 12 tables?
items.a: Probably not for the floor plan alone. It starts paying off with multiple servers, a mix of walk-ins and reservations, or when orders arrive from more than one channel.

items.q: Does QR ordering really speed up turnover?
items.a: It removes the wait between deciding and ordering, which is typically 8–14 minutes and worst at peak. Whether that suits your service style is a separate question worth answering honestly.

items.q: What's the fastest change I can make tomorrow?
items.a: Assign table resets explicitly to a named person for the service. It's free, it takes one sentence at the pre-shift briefing, and it usually recovers five minutes per table.
